newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs call in FBI to help probe bank's failure.
newsitem.headline: Czechs call in FBI to help probe bank's failure.

text.p: The Czech government has asked for help from the Unites States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to help probe the failure of Plzen-based Kreditni Banka a.s., Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said on Friday.
He said Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky had said that the FBI could help with its experience in unwinding the savings and loans failures in the U.S. in the 1980s.

"Governor Tosovsky informed me, that FBI experts were invited because they had troubles with financial criminality with small savings banks in the U.S.," Kocarnik told a news conference. "They managed to find a solution."

The minister said it was necessary to bring in specialists who could sift through the case, such as the probe of debt swaps where complicated derivatives, which bordered "on the edge of the law", were used.
"My opinion in this is, that there should be teams of specialists," Kocarnik said.
In August, the CNB rescinded the licence of the insolvent bank with losses estimated at nearly 12 billion crowns ($450.6 million) after a complicated series of non-performing loans and debt swaps.
On Tuesday, the CNB put another bank, Agrobanka a.s. under forced administration, saying it had become illiquid partly because of its ties to Kreditni and the secretive investment group Motoinvest.
The Czech government, under heavy political pressure from the opposition, has set up a special commission of ministers to lead the investigation of Kreditni's failure,
After the Agrobanka intervention this week, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus reluctantly agreed with the creation of a special parliamentary commission to investigate as well.

Kocarnik rejected any blame for himself or his ministry in the failure of Kreditni, saying that the responsibility lied with the bank's management and it was up to the CNB to watch over the country's banking sector.
The strongest opposition party, the Social Democrats, has repeatedly called for Kocarnik's resignation in the aftermath of the Agrobank intervention.
"The measures of the Finance Ministry are limited on the co-signing of banking licences, and the same thing is true for (the licence's) cancellation," Kocarnik said on Friday.
But when asked on how his ministry's oversight of the capital markets entered the equation, he said: "The sitauation on the capital market regarding transparency is improving."
Czech analysts have repeatedly complained about the opaque nature of securities deals, and have criticised Kocarnik's ministry for being understaffed and slow to react to incidents in the markets.

Kocarnik pointed out that the capital market in the Czech Republic will, for some time, bear marks of the mass voucher-based privatisation, which gave millions of citizens shares in Czech companies between 1991 and 1994.
He said the unwieldy nature of the privatisation created a specific case in the Czech Republic, "but this will dissappear."
